subTopicTitle: Ad Hoc Committees, Joint Parliamentary Committees (JPC) & Select Committees in Parliamentary Oversight

prelimsCapsule.coreConceptSummary: Ad hoc committees are temporary panels appointed for a specific purpose, ceasing to exist upon completing their task and submitting a report. They include Inquiry Committees and Select/Joint Committees on Bills. A Joint Parliamentary Committee (JPC) is an ad hoc body set up by a motion passed in both Houses of Parliament for detailed scrutiny of a complex bill or a specific financial/policy scam, whereas a Select Committee comprises members of only one House.
highYieldFacts: Fact 1: JPCs are constituted by a joint motion of both Houses of Parliament, with a Lok Sabha to Rajya Sabha member ratio typically of 2:1.
Fact 2: The Speaker of Lok Sabha appoints the Chairperson of a JPC if the Lok Sabha initiates it, and the committee has the power to summon witnesses, record evidence, and requisition public records.
Fact 3: Unlike Standing Committees (e.g., Department-related Standing Committees), Ad hoc committees have no permanent existence and dissolve immediately after presenting their reports.
Fact 4: Select Committees examine a specific Bill referred to them and consist of members from a single House (either Lok Sabha or Rajya Sabha).
Fact 5: Recommendations of parliamentary committees, including JPCs, are advisory in nature and not legally binding on the government, though they carry immense moral and political weight.
trapsAndElimination: Trap 1: Confusing JPCs with Department-related Standing Committees (DRSCs). DRSCs are permanent, regular standing committees, whereas JPCs are purely ad hoc and temporary.
Trap 2: Assuming the recommendations of a JPC or Select Committee are binding on the executive. They are strictly recommendatory and advisory.
keyArticlesOrStatutes: Article 105 (Powers, Privileges, etc., of the Houses of Parliament and of the members and committees thereof)

mainsFramework.inDepthTheoryHtml:
Evolution and Significance of Ad Hoc Parliamentary Committees

Parliamentary oversight in modern democracies is increasingly constrained by limited legislative time, complex socio-economic legislations, and partisan majorities. To bridge this gap, parliamentary committees—specifically temporary or ad hoc committees like Joint Parliamentary Committees (JPCs) and Select/Joint Committees on Bills—act as 'mini-parliaments' where detailed, non-partisan scrutiny occurs away from the glare of political grandstanding.

Institutional Architecture of JPCs and Select Committees

  • Joint Parliamentary Committees (JPCs): Created via a motion adopted by one House and concurred in by the other. They are empowered to examine specific bills (like the Joint Committee on the Personal Data Protection Bill or the recent Forest Conservation Amendment Bill) or probe matters of national import (such as the 2G spectrum scam or Bofors).
  • Select Committees: Formed exclusively by members of a single House when a specific Bill is referred to it for clause-by-clause examination, enabling rigorous expert stakeholder consultations.
  • Ad Hoc Inquiry Committees: Constituted on specific ad-hoc demands to investigate particular incidents, though rare in recent decades due to the preference for Judicial Commissions or JPCs.

Contemporary Governance Bottlenecks and Challenges

Despite their intended role as bulomarks of executive accountability, ad hoc committees face structural hurdles:

  • Decline in Referral to Committees: A disturbing legislative trend shows a sharp drop in Bills referred to Select Committees or Joint Committees, with major legislations rushed through Parliament without deep scrutiny.
  • Partisan Polarization: Committee proceedings, historically known for consensus-building, increasingly mirror polarized floor dynamics, weakening objective oversight.
  • Non-Binding Nature of Recommendations: The executive is not mandated to accept committee reports, often leading to watered-down amendments or wholesale dismissal of expert consensus.
  • Lack of Independent Research Support: Committees lack permanent, specialized research staff equivalent to the Congressional Research Service in the US, limiting their capacity to analyze complex economic or technological data.

dimensions.constitutional_or_legal: Grounded in Parliamentary Rules of Procedure (Rule 125 of Lok Sabha Rules) and Article 105 regarding committee privileges.
dimensions.socio_economic: Crucial for safeguarding marginalized groups, consumer rights, and data privacy by incorporating inputs from civil society and domain experts.
dimensions.administrative_governance: Ensures executive accountability, bureaucratic transparency, and prevents hasty, poorly drafted legislation that triggers litigation.
dimensions.international_or_comparative: Mirrors the UK Select Committee system and US Congressional committees, serving as a core index of robust legislative oversight.

landmarkJudgmentsOrReports: National Commission to Review the Working of the Constitution (NCRWC, 2002) recommendations on strengthening parliamentary committee oversight.

modelMainsQA.question: Evaluate the efficacy of Ad Hoc Parliamentary Committees, particularly Joint Parliamentary Committees (JPCs) and Select Committees, in strengthening legislative oversight and checking executive overreach in India. (250 Words, 15 Marks)

approach.intro: Define Ad Hoc Parliamentary Committees (JPCs and Select Committees) and state their constitutional basis under Parliamentary Rules and Article 105.
approach.body: Analyze their specific role in legislative scrutiny, expert consultation, and probing scams. Highlight contemporary challenges (decline in referrals, partisanship, non-binding nature).
approach.conclusion: Suggest institutional safeguards, mandatory committee scrutiny for complex bills, and empowering secretarial support to restore legislative primacy.

modelMainsQA.modelAnswerHtml:
Ad hoc parliamentary committees—comprising Select Committees (single House) and Joint Parliamentary Committees (JPCs) (bicameral)—are temporary bodies constituted for specific legislative scrutiny or investigating national scams. Operating outside the glare of partisan floor politics, they function as the vital institutional anchor of parliamentary oversight in India.

Efficacy in Legislative Oversight and Accountability:

  • In-depth Scrutiny: Unlike rushed floor debates, ad hoc committees enable clause-by-clause examination of complex legislations (e.g., the Joint Committee on Data Protection Bill).
  • Expert and Stakeholder Consultations: They empower civil society, domain experts, industry bodies, and marginalized groups to depose before lawmakers, democratizing law-making.
  • Investigative Power: JPCs possess powers to summon witnesses, inspect confidential government files, and examine public records, acting as an effective check on executive excesses (e.g., past JPCs on the 2G Scam and Joint Stock Exchange scams).

Structural Challenges and Limitations:

  • Decline in Referrals: Recent legislative sessions indicate a worrying trend where major economic and social bills are rushed through Parliament without being referred to Select or Joint Committees.
  • Non-Binding Recommendations: Committee recommendations are purely advisory; the executive often ignores critical amendments suggested by consensus panels.
  • Rising political polarization has occasionally transformed objective inquiry rooms into extensions of partisan battles.

Way Forward: To uphold constitutional morality and deliberative democracy, Parliament must adopt a convention mandating committee scrutiny for all significant public bills. Enhancing independent research staff support and ensuring bipartisan leadership in ad hoc committees will revitalize their role as bulwarks of accountability in India's parliamentary democracy.

practiceMCQs.question:
Consider the following statements regarding Joint Parliamentary Committees (JPCs) in India:
1. A JPC is set up by a joint motion passed in both Houses of Parliament.
2. The recommendations of a JPC are legally binding on the Union Government.
3. Members of a JPC are drawn exclusively from the Lok Sabha.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
practiceMCQs.explanation: Statement 1 is correct: A JPC is constituted by a joint motion of both Houses. Statement 2 is incorrect: Recommendations of JPCs are strictly advisory and not legally binding. Statement 3 is incorrect: JPCs consist of members from both Lok Sabha (usually in a 2:1 ratio) and Rajya Sabha.

practiceMCQs.question: Which of the following best distinguishes a Select Committee from a Joint Parliamentary Committee (JPC)?
options: Select Committees are permanent bodies, whereas JPCs are ad hoc.
Select Committees comprise members from only one House, whereas JPCs comprise members from both Houses.
Select Committees can probe financial scams, whereas JPCs can only examine bills.
Select Committees are chaired exclusively by the Prime Minister, whereas JPCs are chaired by the Speaker.
practiceMCQs.answer: Select Committees comprise members from only one House, whereas JPCs comprise members from both Houses.
practiceMCQs.explanation: A Select Committee is constituted for examining a specific Bill and consists of members from only one House (either Lok Sabha or Rajya Sabha). A Joint Parliamentary Committee (JPC) draws members from both Houses of Parliament.
